overview.text: Helium (He), atomic number 2, is a colorless, chemically unreactive gas and the lightest noble gas. Its name reflects an unusual history: astronomers identified it in sunlight in 1868, before it was confirmed on Earth in 1895. In stars, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing energy; later in some stars, helium can fuse into carbon. On Earth, helium’s low density lets it lift balloons, while its very low boiling point makes liquid helium useful for cooling superconducting magnets in MRI scanners. Helium–neon lasers also scan barcodes. These varied roles—from a product of stellar fusion to a specialized coolant—make helium important in astronomy, medicine, and technology.

key_facts.text: Helium is element 2 in Group 18; it is colorless and chemically unreactive.
Astronomers observed helium’s spectral signature in the Sun in 1868; it was confirmed on Earth in 1895.
Hydrogen fusion produces helium in stars. In later stages of some stars, helium fusion can produce carbon.
Liquid helium cools superconducting magnets in MRI scanners; helium–neon lasers are used to scan barcodes.
Because helium has low density, it is used to fill decorative and weather balloons.
